groups.point: DNA’s authority and neighboring reforms turn on redistributing access to later scrutiny through durable records, while expert judgment remains.
Narcotics retains crystals to meet legal deadlines with limited capacity; replacing its routine method imposes costs that technical availability alone does not resolve.
Forensic biology should be another evaluated case of collective judgment, rather than the analytical reference point outside the comparison.
Firearms already adapted by making judgments reviewable; distinguishing documentary additions from replacement of judgment reveals selective accommodation obscured by the resistance category.
Shared audiences do not locate the spillover boundary: toxicology may fall outside it despite belonging to the same laboratory.
Narcotics’ apparent resistance is a provisional stage of an unresolved rulemaking and capacity problem, without a demonstrated refusal of a binding demand.
Credible local consequences determine whether units change; differences in exposure explain outcomes more directly than occupational values.
Narcotics’ dispute concerns regional control over compulsory standards, with DNA prestige strengthening one coalition’s established methods.
Staff placement and movement toward preferred work help produce occupational cultures, so observed values and responses partly reflect selective membership.
Prior accreditation obligations explain toxicology’s reporting reform; impending litigation accelerates a change whose content and eventual adoption were already established.
Responses protect occupational standing and members’ irreplaceability, making status and power central to the pattern across units.
Explicit DNA comparison in firearms and independently sourced demands elsewhere are combined under one spillover label, obscuring differences in what prompted evaluation.
Across all three units, equipment, data, time, and deadline costs determine responses, while occupational values articulate those practical constraints.
